articles.title: Impact of acoustic property uncertainty on transcranial ultrasound simulation
articles.content: Subject-specific simulations of wave propagation are commonly used to plan and report acoustic and thermal exposure during transcranial ultrasound (TUS) interventions. Their accuracy depends on acoustic and thermal tissue property assumptions, including sound speed, density, and attenuation. Reported property measurements vary widely across the literature, precluding consensus point estimates for simulation. How this property uncertainty affects estimated exposure has not been quantified. We compile literature-based bounds for seven acoustic and thermal properties of skull and brain tissue and assess their individual impact on simulated intensity and temperature rise using two independent simulation platforms (PRESTUS/k-Wave and BabelBrain). Variations in skull attenuation and absorption produced the largest outcome uncertainty: peak intensity in the brain varied roughly threefold across the reported range of skull attenuation alone, while absorption most strongly affected temperature rise within the skull. The direction of each parameter's effect was consistent across platforms and, with one exception, across skull thickness. This allowed bounds to be combined into setups that bracket transmission and temperature rise. Compared to these extremes, default property sets of three simulation toolboxes (k-Plan, BabelBrain, PRESTUS) yielded similar brain intensity but divergent skull heating, driven mainly by differing assumptions on skull absorption and heat capacity. These results indicate that uncertainty in skull acoustic properties is a major source of variability in TUS exposure estimates, and that refined measurements of these properties, together with explicit reporting of exposure uncertainty, are needed to support safe, effective, and reproducible transcranial ultrasound planning.

articles.title: Facing the waves of negative mood: Trait mindfulness moderates the links between physiology and emotion
articles.content: Trait mindfulness is a dispositional ability characterized by awareness, non-judgment, and acceptance of internal and external experiences. Stress is associated with numerous psychological and physical health concerns including depression and anxiety. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have consistently been shown to reduce perceived stress and improve a variety of other health outcomes. However, the mechanisms through which mindfulness confers these benefits are not yet fully understood. This study aimed to examine (1) the relationship between trait mindfulness and changes in cortisol following a negative Mood Induction Procedure (MIP) and (2) whether trait mindfulness moderates the relationship between changes in cortisol and mood reactivity following a negative MIP. Participants were recruited from the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex (N = 25 participants) and completed a series of self-report questionnaires, negative and positive mood induction, and mood assessments. Participants provided salivary cortisol samples before and after negative MIPs. Results indicated that, following the negative MIP, sadness and anxiety were associated with greater reductions in cortisol. Trait mindfulness moderated these associations. Overall, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of emotional responses to negatively-valenced stressors and how they are mitigated by mindfulness. They suggest support for future applications of mindfulness-based interventions in high-stress populations.

articles.title: The association between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older adults: a scoping review
articles.content: BackgroundMental disorders are increasingly prevalent among older adults, significantly affecting their quality of life and overall wellbeing. Recent evidence suggests that dietary factors, particularly protein intake, may play a role in mental health outcomes. However, the association between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older adults remains underexplored. This scoping review aims to examine the relationship between dietary protein intake and mental disorders among older adults.MethodsThis scoping review was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A comprehensive search was performed in three databases (PubMed, Scopus, and ProQuest Health) using predefined keywords and Boolean operators. The inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria were established. Thematic analysis was performed to synthesize and map the evidence across the included studies.ResultsFrom an initial 2,144 records, 13 articles (n = 13) involving older adults were included. Three themes emerged from the thematic analysis: (1) Animal Protein; (2) Plant-Derived Protein; and (3) Mixed Proteins. Both animal and plant protein sources were examined, with generally favourable associations reported for cognitive health. However, findings were inconsistent, particularly for total protein intake, and varied according to protein source and mental or cognitive outcome.DiscussionAssociations between dietary protein intake and mental disorders in older populations are heavily dependent on specific protein sources and the synergistic whole-food matrix rather than the isolated protein quantity. While diverse high-quality protein consumption correlates with preserved mental health, the associations may concurrently reflect residual confounding from healthy-user biases and socioeconomic advantages. The cross-sectional design and lack of quality assessment limit causal inference. Thus, robust longitudinal research and targeted intervention studies are warranted to elucidate the independent neurobiological mechanisms of distinct dietary proteins from overarching dietary patterns.

articles.title: MA-Pose and DMMS-GCN: skeleton-based martial-arts category recognition with edge-device deployment
articles.content: With the development of visual sensor technology and human pose estimation algorithms, skeleton-based action recognition has received extensive attention in sports analysis and training systems. The recognition of martial-arts actions is difficult because different styles can share similar poses while differing in rhythm and coordination. To support this task, we constructed the Martial Arts Pose (MA-Pose) dataset, which contains 433 source videos across 13 martial arts categories. The 33-landmark sequences include normalized image coordinates and monocular relative depth rather than metric 3D ground truth. We further propose a Dynamic Multi-Stream Multi-Scale Graph Convolutional Network (DMMS-GCN), which integrates joint, bone, and motion features. The model combines physical, learnable, and input-adaptive graph topology with parallel temporal convolutions. With a fixed seed of 42, 346 videos are used for training and 87 for validation, with one center crop and one prediction per validation video. DMMS-GCN correctly classifies 73/87 videos (83.91% Top-1; 83.51% Macro-F1; 95% Wilson confidence interval, 74.78%–90.17%) and retrieves the correct class among the top five for 84/87 videos (96.55%). These values describe development-set performance because model selection and evaluation use the same validation subset. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, pose extraction runs at approximately 10 frames/s and classification of a prepared 150-frame tensor takes approximately 120 ms. Collecting the first 150 processed pose frames takes about 15 s, so the deployment demonstrates edge-device feasibility rather than instantaneous recognition. The source code, model checkpoint, and MA-Pose dataset are publicly available.
articles.author: Shilin Guo

articles.title: A purinergic receptor dominance model for microglial state transitions: balancing perturbation and restraint during neuroinflammation
articles.content: Microglia show substantial functional heterogeneity during neuroinflammatory responses, yet the upstream mechanisms through which they interpret extracellular perturbation-associated signals and transition between functional states remain incompletely understood. Purinergic signaling is well positioned to serve as such an environmental sensing system because ATP is released rapidly from stressed or damaged cells and is subsequently metabolized to adenosine, generating an extracellular purine landscape that changes with the magnitude and persistence of tissue stress. We propose a Purinergic Receptor Dominance Model for microglial state transitions during neuroinflammation. Microglial responses are shaped by the changing balance among ATP- and adenosine-sensitive receptor systems. P2Y12-associated signaling supports physiological surveillance; P2X4 contributes to early injury responses; and A1 and A2A receptors provide temporally layered adenosine-linked regulation. Persistent or severe stress may recruit P2X7-associated inflammatory amplification. Under the high-adenosine conditions that can accompany prolonged stress or hypoxia, A2B-linked signaling may also become relevant. The model focuses on the upstream receptor systems through which microglia may gauge the intensity, duration, and metabolic context of tissue stress. It is presented as a testable organizing hypothesis that can be evaluated, refined, or rejected experimentally.
articles.author: Minke Tang

articles.title: The butyrate-m6A-BDNF axis: a hypothesis of gut-brain signal transduction in PSD
articles.content: A reduction in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) protein levels has been reported in post-stroke depression (PSD). However, whether transcript abundance and translation efficiency change in parallel or become uncoupled in PSD remains to be determined. In addition to classical transcriptional regulation by histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, pathological processes may affect BDNF translation independently of transcription, but the relevant epitranscriptomic pathways remain unresolved. Drawing on reports that butyrate can influence m6A-related processes in peripheral tissues and that YTHDF1-dependent translation operates in adult hippocampus and cellular systems, this article proposes the “butyrate–m6A–BDNF” axis as a testable hypothesis. The hypothesis predicts that post-stroke changes in butyrate availability could alter central m6A regulation and thereby affect translation of a biologically motivated candidate transcript such as BDNF. The framework separates established mechanisms, cross-model evidence, and predictions that require direct measurement. The validation plan includes future exposure-resolved, genetic, and cell-type-specific studies; no validation experiments are presented here.
articles.author: Dajun Gu

articles.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
articles.content: Objective. Speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach. Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results. We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. Contributing periods of EEG-based decoding partially overlapped between overt and minimally overt speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance. Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.

articles.title: Diff-ADN: a diffusion-guided artifact denoising network with deterministic residual refinement for EEG
articles.content: Objective. Physiological artifacts degrade electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings and can affect downstream brain–computer interface (BCI) analysis. This study develops a compact single-channel framework for ocular, muscular, cardiac, and mixed-artifact removal. Approach. The Diffusion-Guided Artifact Denoising Network (Diff-ADN) employs a two-stage framework comprising severity-conditioned Stage-I reconstruction followed by diffusion-guided Stage-II residual refinement. During training, forward noising and velocity prediction supervise the Stage-II encoder, whereas inference requires only a single deterministic residual correction, without iterative reverse-diffusion sampling. The framework was evaluated under contamination levels ranging from to dB, using independently recorded artifact sources and motor-imagery decoding across four public EEG datasets. Main results. Diff-ADN achieved mean Pearson correlations of 0.936, 0.839, 0.886, and 0.844 for electrooculographic (EOG),electromyographic (EMG), electrocardiographic (ECG), and mixed EOG+EMG artifacts, respectively. When tested with independently recorded artifact sources, performance varied by artifact type: larger reductions were observed for EOG and EMG, while PTB and INCART ECG differed from the MIT–BIH reference by 0.026 and 0.014, respectively. Across the four motor-imagery datasets, ECG denoising recovered 4.88–5.59 percentage points (pp) in decoding accuracy compared with artifact-corrupted EEG. The largest recovery was 21.90 pp for PTB ECG artifacts on BCI IV-2a at dB. Significance. The proposed framework combines artifact-aware EEG reconstruction with efficient deterministic inference, processing 2 s segments in 12.52–17.08 ms on the tested CPU. Results across independent artifact sources and multiple motor-imagery datasets further show that improvements in waveform reconstruction do not necessarily translate into uniform recovery of BCI decoding accuracy.

articles.title: Human cortical high-gamma power scales with movement rate in healthy participants and stroke survivors
articles.content: Motor cortical high-gamma oscillations (60-90 Hz) occur at movement onset and are spatially focused over the contralateral primary motor cortex.
